name: Oxygen
aliases: O2, dioxygen, medical oxygen, canned oxygen, oxygen bar
summary: Oxygen (O₂) is the gas the body runs on, about 21% of the air. The lungs pass it into the blood, where haemoglobin carries it to every cell to release the energy in food, and without it the brain is harmed within minutes. It has no colour, smell or taste. A healthy person’s blood is already 95 to 100% full of it on ordinary air, so breathing extra oxygen does nothing for them.

uses.text: Medical oxygen, from a cylinder or a concentrator and measured in litres a minute, is given when the blood is short of it: in pneumonia, COPD and severe asthma, after a heart attack or near drowning, and for carbon monoxide poisoning. In hospitals and ambulances nitrous oxide is given mixed with it (Entonox is half and half), so the gas never leaves the lungs short of oxygen. Climbers above about 8,000 m breathe it because the thin air holds too little, and divers breathe air with extra oxygen in it (nitrox), within a depth limit. Canned oxygen and oxygen bars, sold for energy, hangovers or recovery, give a few breaths that are gone from the blood a minute later: there’s no good evidence they do anything for a healthy person.

advisory: Nitrous oxide breathed straight from a balloon takes the place of oxygen in the lungs. Breathing it again and again with no air in between, from a bag or a mask over the face, or in a car or a small closed room can starve the brain of oxygen: people have passed out and died this way. Sit down, take a few normal breaths of air between balloons, and never put anything over the face. Medical nitrous is never given with less than 30% oxygen for this reason.

warnings.text: Too much, for too long, harms. Near pure oxygen breathed for more than about a day can inflame the lungs, and under pressure, in a dive deeper than the gas allows or a hyperbaric chamber, it can bring on a seizure with no warning. Some people with COPD breathe less on high-flow oxygen and build up carbon dioxide, so oxygen at home is breathed at the rate it’s prescribed, not more.

Oxygen doesn’t burn, but everything burns faster and hotter in it, and hair, clothes and bedding soaked in it catch fire easily. No smoking, vaping, candles or gas cookers near a cylinder or concentrator, no oil or grease on its fittings, and water-based creams instead of petroleum jelly under a mask.
